# 🛰️ First Satellite vs. Latest Satellite

## 🔴 Sputnik 1 — The First (1957)

Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite, launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**.

- **Size & Shape:** It was a polished metal sphere **58 cm (23 in) in diameter** with four external radio antennas to broadcast radio pulses.
- **Weight:** Sputnik 1 weighed **83.6 kg (184 pounds)**.
- **Orbit:** Its orbit was elliptical, approximately **230 km** from Earth at its closest point (perigee) and **940 km** at its furthest point (apogee). It took just under an hour and a half to circle the entire planet.
- **Technology & Payload:** It was an extremely simple satellite — a metal sphere with four long antennas. It contained a thermometer, a fan, a radio transmitter, batteries, and little else.
- **Lifespan:** It sent a radio signal back to Earth for **three weeks** before its batteries became depleted. Aerodynamic drag caused it to fall back into the atmosphere on **January 4, 1958**.
- **Total distance traveled:** The orbit of the satellite was observed to decay **92 days after launch**, after having completed about **1,400 orbits** of the Earth over a cumulative distance of **70 million kilometers**.
- **Purpose:** The only cargo onboard Sputnik was a low-power **radio transmitter**, which broadcast a beeping noise at regular intervals.
- **Historical Impact:** Its success was unanticipated by the United States, which precipitated the **Sputnik crisis** and triggered the start of the **Space Race**.

---

## 🟢 ViaSat-3 F3 — Among the Latest (2026)

SpaceX launched the final ViaSat-3 satellite to complete Viasat's trio of high-capacity **Geostationary Orbit (GEO)** satellites. The heavy-lift mission launched on a **Falcon Heavy** from Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida.

- **Launch Date:** **April 27, 2026**.
- **Platform:** Built on **Boeing's high-power 702MP+ platform** and integrated at Boeing's El Segundo facility in California.
- **Orbit:** Launched via Falcon Heavy, it uses electric propulsion to place itself into **geostationary orbit**.
- **Capacity:** Designed to deliver over **1 Terabit per second (Tbps)** of throughput capacity, leveraging innovative payload design and advanced beam-forming technology to optimize and steer immense capacity in real time.
- **Coverage:** ViaSat-3 F3 is designed to provide regional coverage over the **Asia-Pacific (APAC) region**.
- **Services:** The satellite provides **broadband connectivity** with speeds of 100+ Mbps to homes, businesses, commercial aircraft, government/defense markets, and maritime enterprises.
- **Users:** Its flexible bandwidth capabilities are a significant differentiator for **commercial mobility and defense** customers as demand for resilient, high-quality satellite communication services continues to accelerate.
- **Service Entry:** The satellite is expected to enter service by **late summer 2026**.

---

| Feature | 🔴 Sputnik 1 (1957) | 🟢 ViaSat-3 F3 (2026) |
|---|---|---|
| **Launch Date** | October 4, 1957 | April 27, 2026 |
| **Country/Operator** | Soviet Union | Viasat, Inc. (USA) |
| **Launch Vehicle** | R-7 Rocket | SpaceX Falcon Heavy |
| **Mass** | 83.6 kg | Thousands of kg (702MP+ bus) |
| **Orbit Type** | Low Earth Orbit (LEO) | Geostationary Orbit (GEO) |
| **Shape/Design** | Simple metal sphere | Advanced multi-reflector platform |
| **Payload** | Basic radio transmitter | 1+ Tbps broadband internet payload |
| **Mission Life** | ~3 months | Many years (commercial satellite) |
| **Technology** | Thermometer, batteries, radio | Advanced beamforming, electric propulsion |
| **Purpose** | Prove orbit was possible | Global broadband internet & defense comms |
| **Impact** | Started the Space Race | Completes global satellite internet coverage |

---

The contrast is staggering — in under **70 years**, humanity went from a simple beeping metal ball orbiting Earth for a few months, to a multi-ton, AI-steered, terabit-capable communications satellite serving millions of users across an entire ocean region. 🚀
